tweets.text:
US homebuyers are walking away from deals at the highest rate in years:

14.0% of home-purchase agreements that went under contract fell through in July, the highest rate since November 2023.

The national cancellation rate has held between 13.0% and 14.0% over the last 4 years, well above the lower rates typical of the seller's market from 2020 to 2022.

Atlanta posted the highest cancellation rate last month, at 19.8%, followed by Houston at 19.6%, San Antonio at 18.7%, and Las Vegas at 18.6%.

This comes as sellers outnumber buyers by ~51%, near the highest percentage on record, giving buyers more options and making them more willing to walk away over inspection issues, low appraisals, or rejected concessions.

At the same time, high home prices and elevated mortgage rates are leaving buyers with less financial room, making unexpected costs or concerns about taking on large monthly payments more likely to derail deals.

The housing market is under historic pressure.

Non-asset owners are very worried about inflation.

The 3-month moving average of 1-year inflation expectations among US consumers with no stock holdings hit ~5.0% in August, near the highest level this year.

This is significantly above the ~3.0% recorded in late 2024.

Meanwhile, the 3-month moving average of inflation expectations among US consumers with the largest stock holdings remained below 4.0% last month.

Readings for both groups were roughly in-line with levels seen in late-2022, following the recovery from the energy crisis.

Asset owners are the only winners in this economy.

tweets.text:
Japan just printed its fastest wage growth since 1997. For global markets, that is a lit fuse.

Nominal pay rose 4.7% in July, the biggest jump in nearly three decades and a mile above the 3.8% expected. It hands the Bank of Japan the cover to hike again next week, a move markets have already priced.

Now the intermarket chain. A hiking BOJ narrows the rate gap that funded the yen carry trade for a decade. This wage print is the fundamental fuel under the yen rally that just topped the intervention high. Yen up, carry trade unwinds, and the selling lands on US tech and global risk. August 2024 was the rehearsal.

One catch the bulls will ignore. Japanese households cut spending for an eighth straight month even as pay surged, and September's food price hikes trace to oil and a weak yen. So the BOJ is tightening into a consumer that will not spend, which makes the currency the real transmission belt. Watch USD/JPY into Sept 18. That is where a Tokyo wage number becomes a Wall Street problem.

Nominal pay rose 4.7% in July, the biggest jump in nearly three decades and a mile above the 3.8% expected. It hands the Bank of Japan the cover to hike again next week, a move markets have already priced.

Now the intermarket chain. A hiking BOJ narrows the rate gap that funded the yen carry trade for a decade. This wage print is the fundamental fuel under the yen rally that just topped the intervention high. Yen up, carry trade unwinds, and the selling lands on US tech and global risk. August 2024 was the rehearsal.

One catch the bulls will ignore. Japanese households cut spending for an eighth straight month even as pay surged, and September's food price hikes trace to oil and a weak yen. So the BOJ is tightening into a consumer that will not spend, which makes the currency the real transmission belt. Watch USD/JPY into Sept 18. That is where a Tokyo wage number becomes a Wall Street problem.

Trump keeps calling Canada's trade surplus with the US 'unacceptable.' The chart shows how thin Canada's hand really is.

Strip out energy and Canada runs a trade deficit with the US. The entire surplus Washington is angry about is oil and gas, and it has been shrinking since Trump's election and the 25% tariff threat.

Canada is escalating anyway. On Tuesday it hits hundreds of US products with tariffs of 15% to 50%, steel jumping to 50%, aimed at Michigan and Ohio ahead of the midterms. Washington is already threatening 50% auto tariffs on Jan 1.

Here is what a tariff actually does. It delivers a one-time price shock and distorts trade flows, and it never creates sustained inflation. Oxford Economics pegs the hit to Canadian output at 0.3%, with layoffs already rising in export industries. The damage lands on Canadian growth and the loonie, and on US exporters into Michigan and Ohio. Watch the loonie and the TSX. That is where a trade war gets paid for.

Tokyo and Washington spent a fortune defending the yen. The market just smashed through the floor their intervention built.

The yen hit its strongest since February, breaking below 155 and topping the 155.23 high set after the coordinated US-Japan intervention. Up 2.4% in a week. The first intervention fizzled. This leg is organic, powered by bets the Bank of Japan hikes on Sept 18, possibly back to back.

Here is why a Tokyo currency move is your problem. The yen is the world's funding currency. For years traders borrowed it near zero to buy US tech and global risk, the carry trade. When the yen rips higher and stop-losses below 155 cascade, that trade unwinds and the selling hits the assets it financed. The August 2024 mini-crash was the preview.

Central-bank firepower is losing its grip, and the carry trade is the next domino. Watch USD/JPY into the BOJ's Sept 18 meeting. A hawkish BOJ that keeps the yen bid is how a Japanese rate decision becomes a Wall Street selloff.

The Fed hiked over 500 basis points and the economy refused to break. One chart explains why.

Corporate America locked in record-low fixed rates during the pandemic and cut its net interest bill to 0.4% of GDP. The Treasury did the opposite. It never termed out its debt at zero, and now pays 3.6% of GDP in interest.

The whole cost of higher rates landed on the government's balance sheet while corporate America skated. That is the transmission mechanism that went missing after 2022, and why tightening never slowed the economy.

The corporate cushion has an expiration date. Pandemic-era debt is rolling into higher coupons, and the hit lands hardest on the most levered, cash-poor borrowers: leveraged software and junk credit at the front of the line. Favor quality balance sheets over levered stories. Leverage that felt free at 2% becomes a wrecking ball at 6%, and the maturity wall is the clock.

Copper just hit an all-time high, $14,533 a ton. Read the reason before you call it inflation.

This record was manufactured by a tariff threat. Traders front-running possible US copper levies shipped hundreds of thousands of tons into American warehouses to capture the Comex premium, drained the LME's global stockpiles to critical lows, and forced a squeeze. Spot now trades above futures, a backwardation that signals scarcity, in a market where physical demand is soft.

That is the whole lesson on tariffs. A tariff is a one-time price shock and a distortion in relative prices, never a source of sustained inflation: one metal, one border, one policy. When Commerce finally rules, the arbitrage closes, the hoarded US metal releases, and the squeeze unwinds. Real inflation comes from the printing press. This came from the customs house.

$CPER

tweets.text:
The great EV transition just threw itself into reverse.

After hundreds of billions in stranded capital chasing a mostly-electric market by the 2030s, the auto industry's new fix for range anxiety is a gas engine. Hyundai, Ford and Jeep-maker Stellantis are rolling out extended-range EVs: a battery car with a gas generator bolted on to recharge it.

The Ram 1500 REV promises up to 690 miles, more than double a typical US EV. Ford is resurrecting the electric F-150 Lightning it killed last December, this time with a gas engine. Hyundai's Santa Fe version targets 600 miles in 2027.

Here is the lesson for every policy-driven boom. EV sales sank the moment the $7,500 subsidy went away. Mandates and incentives can pull an industry's capex forward by years, but when the check stops, real demand reasserts itself and the stranded assets land on shareholders. The same script is being written right now in AI and solar.

This observation is in line with what I recently wrote in our report: 

"The problem is that China's high-tech sectors remain a relatively small part of the overall economy and have a high barrier to entry. The vast majority of the population therefore remains largely excluded from this new growth cycle."

"For ordinary households working in traditional manufacturing and service industries—restaurants, transportation, construction, retail, and countless other parts of the domestic economy—the reality remains very different. These sectors continue to face deflation, shrinking margins, weak income growth, and rising bankruptcies. In other words, while the upper end of the K is enjoying an extraordinary boom, the lower end—which represents the overwhelming majority of the population—is dealing with a recession."

"This is the fundamental political problem created by China's K-shaped development model: the gains are highly concentrated, while the pain is widely distributed. Ultimately, we believe the social backlash from the lower end of the K is likely to become increasingly difficult for Beijing to ignore."
